topic_summaries.Rewilding, Biodiversity and Sustainable:
• The Guardian dominates coverage, framing rewilding and biodiversity loss through concrete, solutions-focused stories — heritage farming, drought resilience, and migratory bird decline — while BBC takes a more reactive, threat-based angle (extinctions, Chester Zoo pipeline)
• The Guardian and BBC both cover climate impacts on wildlife but differ in tone: The Guardian emphasises human adaptation and land stewardship; BBC foregrounds institutional responses to crisis
• The Independent raises a rare critical angle on green energy's ecological trade-offs (solar expansion harming birds in China); Metro's sole article is entirely off-topic
topic_summaries.North Sea Oil and Gas Debate:
• The Guardian frames North Sea development as economically self-defeating and climatically damaging, citing expert analysis; GB News focuses on job losses, political dithering, and criticism of Burnham and Labour's delays.

• GB News gives prominent voice to Conservative critics like Badenoch, portraying inaction as harmful to energy security and households; The Guardian's opinion piece acknowledges approval could be justified but only under strict conditions.
topic_summaries.Flooding, Extreme Weather and UK Infrast:
• BBC and Metro lead on immediate flash flooding risk and travel disruption; Evening Standard localises this through Sadiq Khan's warnings for London
• The Guardian frames extreme weather as a systemic, long-term crisis ("climate whiplash," government resilience planning); GB News focuses on practical consumer impacts like hosepipe bans and drought records
• BBC and Evening Standard cover the Network Rail derailment lawsuit as an infrastructure accountability story, while The i highlights sewage alerts and school heatwave unpreparedness as policy failures
topic_summaries.UK Energy Bills and Net Zero Policy:
• GB News dominates coverage of rising energy bills and Net Zero costs, framing them as threats to households, food security, and housebuilding targets; The Guardian focuses on renewable expansion and challenges to climate sceptics like Tice and Musk.

• BBC takes a neutral, local-level lens — covering a council scrapping its climate declaration and a solar farm approval despite public opposition — without the ideological framing seen in GB News or The Guardian.

• Evening Standard occupies a factual, consumer-focused middle ground, reporting the Ofgem price cap rise and fact-checking opposition energy claims, without strong editorial slant.
topic_summaries.Record Ocean Temperatures and Climate Sc:
• BBC and The Guardian lead with precise temperature data (21.1C) and dual causes—human-induced climate change and El Niño; Daily Mail emphasises El Niño alone as the dominant driver
• The Guardian goes beyond reporting to include opinion/advocacy framing, with one piece calling ocean heating "an outrage, not a tragedy" and assigning deliberate human blame
• The Independent focuses on human and marine life consequences; Daily Mail widens coverage to related sea-level rise research, suggesting broader environmental alarm-building
topic_summaries.El Niño Threat and UK Weather Outlook:
• BBC and Met Office-citing outlets (Evening Standard, Metro, The Guardian) frame El Niño as an "unprecedented" scientific event bringing autumn storms and rain to the UK; Daily Mail amplifies this with more alarmist language like "wreak havoc" and "bitterly cold winter"

• The Independent takes the broadest global perspective, covering impacts on Asia, Pakistan, and 2027 temperature records, while also running opinion pieces urging wealthy nations to act

• The Guardian uses El Niño as a springboard for political commentary (Zoe Williams column), whereas most other outlets stay focused on weather forecasting and practical UK impact
topic_summaries.Air Quality, Clean Transport and Urban C:
• The Guardian and Evening Standard both cover ULEZ/clean air zones but from different angles — Guardian asks why cities globally are slow to adopt similar schemes, while Evening Standard and GB News focus on the specific health benefits for London children's lung development
• GB News covers Conservative plans to scrap diesel HGV bans as a taxpayer-saving measure, while also reporting expert criticism of those same plans in a separate piece — reflecting internal tension in its framing
• The Guardian dominates coverage overall, spanning cycling promotion, urban heat, global climate action and US policy rollbacks; BBC and Channel 4 focus more narrowly on localised environmental harms such as Welsh wildfires and illegal waste dumps

Heatwaves show UK must do more to promote cycling and walking, campaigners say


Civil society groups argue climate crisis means transport sector needs to urgently reduce its carbon emissions




Dozens of civil society groups have demanded the UK government do more to promote cycling and walking, after this summer’s extreme heat exposed the desperate need to decarbonise transport.
This summer’s heatwaves and wildfires were “immediate, real-world manifestations of the climate emergency”, the groups said, making reform of transport – responsible for more carbon emissions than any other sector in the UK – an urgent priority.

Last year, domestic transport was responsible for almost a third of the UK’s net greenhouse gas emissions – with the total emissions from the sector increasing 2% over the previous year.







London bus drivers resume strike over heatwave working amid fears over air con deal 

Read more
The groups call for a “modal shift” in transport provision. “What that means is creating the conditions which allow people to travel for a higher proportion of the trip by walking, cycling, public transport and shared mobility than by private cars,” said Ben Plowden, the chief executive of the Campaign for Better Transport.
The demand comes after Labour appeared to have shelved targets for an increase in trips made by public transport and a reduction in trips using private vehicles.
Before the 2024 election, Labour had committed to setting goals for shifting travel habits away from private vehicles and towards public transport and active travel, such as cycling and walking.


But by this summer the government’s cycling and walking strategy had no broader targets to increase the percentage of total trips made by public transport or to reduce the percentage of total trips made by cars.
The intervention, signed by 54 civil society organisations, was led by the Campaign for Better Transport. Plowden said their call had been lent increased urgency by the summer’s repeated heatwaves and the oil price inflation caused by the US war on Iran.
“That such a range of organisations have come together to make this statement shows the urgent need for stronger action in response to the climate emergency, which has had such a devastating impact on communities across the country this summer,” Plowden said.
“The heatwaves and wildfires, the harm to people, nature and infrastructure, are just a taste of things to come if we do not act urgently.”

Households are facing heightened winter pressure from energy bills after regulator Ofgem raised its price cap by 4% to a three-year high

        







Household energy bills to rise 
PA

Matt Watts, News Editor|Nicholas Cecil, Chief Reporter  @nicholascecil
1 minute ago
  

 
COMMENTS







Households will pay more on their energy bills from October after Ofgem raised its price cap by 4% to a three-year high.




The regulator said the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the average household using both electricity and gas if this level was sustained for a year.








It means, in short, that the average annual energy bills will rise by £60 for a typical household in October.




The rise is a blow to millions of households struggling with the cost of living as inflation remains stubbornly high.




While experts have warned households should brace for a double blow, with October’s rise in the energy price cap will likely be followed by another hefty increase in January.




Ofgem's price cap, set every three months, puts a limit on how much suppliers can charge per unit of energy, so homes that use high amounts of energy will pay more than the typical figure announced, and households which use less energy should pay less.











October's price cap will cover the period from 1 October to the end of this year. 


Millions of households in London will be hit with higher energy bills
AFP/Getty




The next cap, covering 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2027, is due to be announced on 25 November.




Ofgem said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas prices as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with volatile global markets remaining the dominant driver of price changes.




Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s director general for markets, said: “High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK.







“We welcome the Government’s intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter.




“Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap, and many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for electricity consumed out of peak times.

Ofgem has confirmed the energy price cap will rise four per cent for a typical household from October, in a decision that lands just as Britons prepare to turn the heating back on.
The new cap takes effect on October 1 and runs until December 31, representing a rise to £1,723 annually, or £60 a year, for the average household, on the current level of £1,663.


Cornwall Insight, whose forecasts are closely tracked in the sector, had predicted a four per cent increase to £1,729 in its final estimate before the announcement; a level that on a unit-for-unit basis would be the highest since July 2023. 
The energy price cap is set by regulator Ofgem every three months and limits the maximum amount suppliers can charge per unit of gas and electricity, plus the daily standing charge — it does not cap a household's total bill, which still depends on how much energy is used.

 Ofgem has made its latest energy price cap announcement  | 
GETTY


It applies to households on standard variable tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales, meaning anyone who has not switched to a fixed deal, while those on fixed contracts and customers in Northern Ireland are unaffected.
Today's figure is measured against Ofgem's revised definition of a typical household, introduced on July 1 to reflect the fact that average energy use has fallen.
The change also coincides with the removal of VAT on domestic electricity from October 1, meaning the headline number is not directly comparable with caps set earlier in the year.

articles.raw_rss: One scientist says there are thousands of sites across the UK that need investigating.

articles.jina_text:
Michael Sheen took up the job of investigating Douglas Gowan's concerns about an international chemical giant dumping carcinogenic waste in Wales





A former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping seal toxic waste underground said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.
Stephen Constance worked at the chemical giant's Newport factory in the 1990s and came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
But the 14 sites identified in the programme are just the tip of the iceberg and there are about 20,000 high-concern sites in the UK, said Dr David Megson, the scientist involved in the documentary.
Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond when asked to comment.
Constance was one of dozens of people who contacted BBC Wales after coverage of Sheen's investigation into Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).
Researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan spent 50 years trying to persuade authorities to investigate what he believed was widespread dumping of industrial chemicals.
These included PCBs, which he called "some of the worst contaminants known to man", and were widely used in the 20th Century, including for lipstick and white goods.
They were banned in the UK in the 1970s and have since been banned by 151 countries.















BBC/Wall to Wall Media
Douglas Gowan spent 50 years trying to make people listen to his concerns about chemical contamination in Wales
Constance, 61, said working for Monsanto was "absolutely dreadful".
Looking back, he said it was "quite evident that nobody was fully appraised of the potential hazard that they were exposed to".
The material was already buried when Constance arrived and it was his job to dig a 6m-deep trench around the outside of the mound before it was sealed using plastic membrane sheets and liquid clay. 
While he believes this prevented airborne contamination, he is unsure if it would have stopped contamination into the Earth due to the high water table linked to the tides.

Stephen Constance
PCB material was covered over with plastic membrane and liquid clay
When asked if he felt safe, he said: "In terms of what we knew was there and what we were potentially exposed to, no."
Constance is in remission from cancer after having follicular lymphoma. 










"I'm not suggesting in any way at all that it's linked, but the thought did cross my mind," he said. 

Stephen Constance
Stephen Constance says he does not feel safe now he knows what chemicals he was exposed to
In the documentary, journalists Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor reveal a memo from Monsanto dated to 1972 which found that it knew PCBs were a danger to human health and was closing its site in the US as a result of legal action from a town. 
However, it then increased its work at the plant in Newport.

Labour will miss its flagship 1.5 million homes target by more than half a million as soaring costs and new Net Zero and building rules cripple housebuilding, a leading construction economist has warned.
A new forecast unveiled today predicts just 940,000 new homes will be built in England over the five-year period - 560,000 short of the Government's ambition, and fewer than the previous two five-year periods.


Despite Labour's promise to "get Britain building", Professor Noble Francis, economics director at the Construction Products Association (CPA) and professor of construction economics at University College London, warned the Government "cannot have it both ways" by demanding more homes while continually piling extra costs onto builders.
He said: "The Government will not get its 1.5 million homes over the next five years."

UK to warn citizens to stock up on food amid threat from climate crisis and hostile states


Government resilience campaign aims to ensure people can cope in a national disaster, in order to free resources for most vulnerable




UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience.
The new campaign from the Cabinet Office will set out ways people can prepare for extreme weather events and potential attacks from hostile states, including stocking up on bottled water, sources told the Guardian.

The aim will be to ensure most households have basic supplies and knowledge about how to cope in a crisis, in order to free up immediate government resources for the most vulnerable.







Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?

Read more
Planning for a number of disasters, from cyber-attacks to extreme heat and flooding, has increased over the past few months after a number of incidents both in the UK and across the world. The plans, first reported by the FT, also include an internal reassessment of government preparations for a military attack by a hostile state affecting Britain.
The Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, who is Andy Burnham’s de-facto deputy, is also understood to be coordinating crisis planning across departments in Whitehall to allow swifter assistance to affected communities.


View image in fullscreen
Drought is predicted to cause food shortages. Photograph: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock
During his campaign to become Makerfield MP, Burnham spoke repeatedly about the threat of flooding to communities and the inadequacy of government planning and response.


Burnham convened a Cobra meeting earlier this month to coordinate the government’s response to the heatwave, amid a threat of spreading wildfires and drought warnings.
The government was criticised, however, for its decision to send an emergency phone alert warning of wildfires last week, which charities and domestic abuse survivors said risked the safety of people who might be hiding secret phones.
Haigh’s predecessor, Darren Jones, had said that work was under way on the so-called “war book” on how international conflict might affect the UK.

articles.jina_text:
How can positive ideas help shape a better world? Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/SOPA Images/Shutterstock/iStockPhoto/REX



There are countless initiatives around the world that can inspire people and spur them into action. Amid the devastation of the climate crisis, our journalists strive to highlight these stories of hope 
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 













 
 
The news is very often about the bad things (especially if you’re on the Guardian’s environment desk). Wildfires, floods, tipping points, billionaires making huge profits and buying themselves island refuges for the apocalypse … And yet, ticking along beside that is the steady pulse of what the rest of humanity is doing in response to the climate crisis. From housing developments with no cars to buildings made out of hemp, all over the planet people are ploughing ahead and changing their neighbourhoods and cities and the world.

But as news stories typically need to be about new developments or things people didn’t previously know about, it can be hard to cover all those brilliant initiatives being undertaken in the background – no matter how cheering they are. Which is why, back in 2023, we decided to ignore the usual rules about what constitutes “news” and start writing about them anyway. Readers, we knew, would like to hear about them.


And so was born the Alternatives, a weekly news column where we cover these different projects. We’re constantly amazed by some of the things we learn. Norway has heat pumps in two-thirds of its homes. China’s sponge cities are targeting 70% rainwater reuse. Paris is building a gigantic cooling machine using river water. It feels as if the series is a vast chronicle of the transformations that are taking place everywhere, far faster than we sometimes realise.
This year, as part of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign, we are highlighting all of the work that our environment team does to bring readers positive ideas such as those above, providing hope that a better world is possible if we start acting on it.
So, we asked our environment reporters around the world to share one big idea from their journalism – funded by you – that has helped drive or inspire some kind of positive change for the planet. Their answers are below.
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 


Petra Stock
Climate and environment reporter, Guardian Australia
Many objections to wind turbines cite the impact on wildlife, such as birds and bats. But there are simple fixes and innovations that demonstrate there doesn’t need to be a trade-off between clean energy and safeguarding biodiversity. One such approach I reported – which involves raising the “cut in” speed at which turbines start spinning – has the potential to save tens of thousands of native bats every year, with minimal impact on energy output.



Ajit Niranjan
European environment correspondent

US fossil fuel lobbyists also represent hundreds of cities fighting for climate damages


Local governments working with firms also linked to fossil fuel giants, analysis of federal lobbying disclosures shows




Congressional lobbyists working for fossil fuel firms that are exacerbating the climate crisis are simultaneously representing more than 300 local governments raising funding to recover from climate damage, according to a new analysis.
The research by F Minus and Make Polluters Pay reviewed congressional lobbying disclosures for the first quarter of 2026, finding that another 568 local governments hired fossil fuel lobbyists to work on non-climate related issues during that time, some of which included climate adjacent issues, like healthcare and home insurance.

Dozens of lobbying firms were identified by researchers as working on both sides of climate action. James Browning, the founder and executive director of F Minus, said local governments who hire these firms to lobby for climate mitigation, disaster relief, and wildlife conservation likely don’t know that the same firms are working for clients like ExxonMobil and the American Petroleum Institute (API), which critics say are pushing to further dependence on fossil fuels. “They are locked into these relationships with big firms and may also not know they are the ones blocking climate efforts,” Browning said.


For example, the analysis shows US multinational law firm Greenberg Traurig has lobbied for three fossil fuel entities (API, ConocoPhillips and the Western States Petroleum Association in California) that have opposed state-level legislation aimed at holding fossil fuel companies financially accountable for their historic climate-warming emissions and using that revenue, in the form of climate superfunds, to support climate mitigation costs. Miami-Dade county, in Florida, hired the firm to lobby for shoreline protection and Everglades restoration. “That’s a glaring conflict,” Browning said.
The mayor of Miami-Dade county didn’t respond to a request for comment about the perceived conflict of interest.

Demonstrators hold up "Stop Data Centers" signs as US President Donald Trump speaks at the General Motors Proving Ground testing facility in Milford, Michigan, US, on Monday, July 27, 2026. Photograph: Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images


Trump EPA aims to exempt datacenters from disclosing air pollution, advocates warn


Trump administration proposes new rule to dismantle requirement for datacenters to publicly report air pollution




A new rule proposed by the Trump administration aims to kill public notification for datacenter air pollution, public health advocates warn, and allow emission permits to be issued behind closed doors.
The datacenters are often sources of nitrogen oxide, which helps form ozone, carbon monoxide and heavy metals, among other pollutants.

The Clean Air Act requires “minor” air polluters to disclose to the public via state agencies how much pollution their proposed project will release, but the proposed new rule from Donald Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) would dismantle that protection for datacenter proposals. Instead, it would make disclosure voluntary at state and some local officials’ discretion.
Many state political establishments support datacenters, and observers say it is unlikely most would voluntarily require big tech to disclose the information. The move is likely intended to curb criticism and public oversight of datacenters, said Joe Goffman, a former assistant administrator for the EPA’s office of air and radiation.


Without this data, communities won’t know what they’re breathing once a datacenter is built, and will have less ability to fight back in court or in public relations battles. Goffman said the Clean Air Act is supposed to offer “an ironclad promise” to give the entire US public a voice on these issues.
“The administration is basically saying: ‘You all may have thought this was an ironclad promise, but it no longer is,’” Goffman added. He co-authored comments on the proposed rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Network. The EPA just closed the public comment period, and the rule could face a legal challenge if finalized.
The move comes amid a national surge in datacenters that are an essential part of the artificial intelligence boom. Many datacenter developers apply for minor pollution source permits for the up to dozens of diesel generators or gas turbines used to help power their facilities, or provide backup generation.

‘Environmental violence’: inside the fight to save indigenous land from becoming a nuclear dumping ground


New documentary To Use a Mountain spotlights the pain and triumph of resisting government efforts to turn parts of rural US into disposal sites




Nuclear energy was supposed to be our salvation, humanity’s chance to retool technology first conceived as a weapon of mass destruction into an engine of limitless prosperity. But even as the industry touted nuclear fission as an economic game-changer (never mind the astronomical startup costs), a safety paragon (never mind the spills at Chornobyl, Three Mile Island and Fukushima) and harmless fodder for an American comedy institution (never mind that glowing rod on Homer’s back or the three-eyed fish), there was no getting around the matter of what to do with all the toxic waste (never mind nuclear’s claimed green credentials).
The stagnant state of that dirty business brought Casey Carter, the director of the new avant-garde documentary called To Use a Mountain, back to his interview with a Washington state farmer who was part of a class-action lawsuit against the government over the release of radioactive material from the Hanford nuclear reservation – site of the world’s first full-scale plutonium production reactor. The farmer’s words still echo, despite ultimately being cut to fit the film’s 90-minute runtime. “He joked that nuclear power is the only faith-based energy because everyone always asks, ‘Do you believe in it?’” Carter says. “He was like, ‘You don’t have to believe in solar. It’s just a pretty good idea.’”




To Use a Mountain could exist as a coda to Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer, showing how the Manhattan Project physicist’s fears about nuclear technology’s vast potential for devastation proved more justified than even he could have imagined. In particular, the film trains its lens on the passage of the 1982 Nuclear Waste Policy Act – which, among other things, placed six rural communities across the US in a derby of sorts to become the permanent site for more than 90,000 tons of high-level nuclear waste.


The plan was for the waste to remain isolated for 10,000 years, and that humans would still be around to celebrate the Reagan-era edict as a triumph. But the affected communities are more inclined to believe there may be no one left to parcel out due credit once the waste leaches into groundwater, pollutes the air and contaminates the food chain. Going with the grain: how restoring biodiversity led one farmer back to heritage wheat


Henry Astor looked back to his grandfather’s time for the inspiration to find older varieties that could help nature on his Cotswold farm




It is the earliest harvest Henry Astor can remember. But walking through the scorched wheatfields of his Cotswolds farm, signs of life are everywhere – swarms of insects, kaleidoscopic wildflower meadows, bushy hedgerows several metres wide. A yellowhammer perches on a nearby tree.
There are 18 other red-listed birds on the farm, says Astor, who this year ringed 23 barn owls, three kestrels, two little owls as well as goshawk chicks. “Last winter we had clouds of goldfinch, chaffinch and greenfinch,” he says. Britain has lost 73 million birds since 1970; but at Bruern Farms, a small but welcome reversal is taking shape.

Between 30,000 and 40,000 trees have been planted over the past decade, many as part of a flood-mitigation scheme, some in a 17-hectare (42-acre) agroforestry section interspersing wheat with heritage fruits such as Cox’s pippin and Blenheim orange apples. Wildflower meadows are rebuilding soil fertility.
As part of his obligations as a member of the North East Cotswold Farmer Cluster, which Astor co-founded, a plot is left for bird feeding, to boost populations. According to the cluster co-chair, Tim Field, this has resulted in flocks of linnets, goldfinch and chaffinch across 40 farms involved in the feeding project, while one farm has seen more than 400 teal feeding among watercress in a wetland area.


View image in fullscreen
Apple trees in a multi-crop field at Bruern Farm. Photograph: Sam Frost/The Guardian
Catastrophic biodiversity loss since the postwar “green revolution” has been well documented. Wheat played its part, as heritage grains and mixed populations gave way to vast monocultures of dwarf wheat. Several initiatives are attempting to reverse course with nature-friendly farming, the farms in Astor’s farmer cluster among them.
In all, Astor and neighbouring farmers have 800 hectares of floodplain meadow under restoration, while 3,000 hectares have been set aside for flood mitigation along the River Evenlode, including Bruern Farms’ land.
Despite this progress, Field is one of those unconvinced by the government’s recently announced “30 by 30” nature restoration plans.

His efforts have attracted 19 red-listed bird species, barn owls, kestrels, and large flocks of finches, representing a small but meaningful reversal of Britain's loss of 73 million birds since 1970. Astor has also returned to growing heritage wheat varieties, milling his own flour and supplying it to bakers, inspired by farming practices from his grandfather's era.

articles.jina_text:

View image in fullscreen
The argument that approving Rosebank and Jackdaw would cut bills and improve energy security is a ‘delusion’, say experts. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images


Climate damage would obliterate any economic benefits of new North Sea fields, analysis shows


Exclusive: Economic harm of CO2 pollution from Rosebank and Jackdaw forecast to far outweigh any boost to UK




The climate damage caused by developing the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields under consideration by the UK government would destroy their economic benefits many times over, according to an analysis.
It estimates the economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would be between £119bn and £336bn in the coming decades, compared with the £28.7bn in value to the UK estimated by Adura, the fossil fuel company promoting the new fields.

The assessment applies peer-reviewed research on how rising temperatures harm economies to the production estimates for the fields from the company. The figures are likely to be underestimates, as they do not include losses from amplified extreme weather, sea level rise or climate deaths. The analysis has been submitted to the Rosebank consultation and to an academic journal.


View image in fullscreen
Protesters last week calling on Andy Burnham to block the plans for Rosebank and Jackdaw. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock
The decision on whether to approve Rosebank and Jackdaw has become highly controversial, with the oil industry, some energy leaders and rightwing political parties pushing for the go-ahead. Most centre and leftwing political parties, climate scientists and environmental campaigners are opposed. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, also faces a revolt from Labour MPs who oppose the plans, while the former energy secretary Ed Miliband once called the Rosebank proposal “climate vandalism”.


The argument that approving Rosebank and Jackdaw would reduce UK bills and improve energy security is a “delusion”, according to energy experts, as they are internationally traded commodities. Proponents of new drilling argue it would boost the UK economy, but the new analysis indicates this would be outweighed by long-term economic damage.
“The numbers presented here show there’s going to be a very strong destruction of [economic] value above and beyond what Rosebank and Jackdaw could generate for the UK,” said Luke Hatton, at Imperial College London, who conducted the analysis. “The alternative is to really double down on clean energy technologies.” The UK’s net zero sector has grown three times faster than the overall UK economy in recent years.

articles.jina_text:

View image in fullscreen
The growing proportion of older people in Europe’s population suggests heat-related deaths on the continent are likely to rise, S&P said. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images


Europe’s heatwaves threaten insurers’ earnings, rating agency S&P says


Rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and illness, especially among older people, could drive up premiums




Europe’s intense heatwaves could hit insurers’ earnings as companies face a rise in claims linked to heat-related deaths and worsening health conditions, the rating agency S&P has said.
While a long summer of extreme heat will have increased drought and wildfire-related claims, the rating agency said there would also be fallout for life and health insurers, and for the reinsurers who provide financial protection to insurance companies.

That could ultimately translate to higher premiums for customers, as insurers try to cover increased payouts to policyholders.
Europe’s heatwaves, paired with its ageing population, have created a perfect storm, with the health impacts of high temperatures falling disproportionately on older people. That fact has resulted in a wave of life insurance claims over heat-related deaths, and increased demand for private medical services, at a time when rising temperatures have not yet been fully reflected in original contracts.


Between 2004 and 2024, the share of people aged 65 and over in the EU rose from 16.4% to 21.6%, while the proportion of those aged 80 and over rose from 3.8% to 6.1%. “The increasing share of elderly people – who are particularly vulnerable to heat stress – suggests that heat-related mortality in Europe is likely to rise,” the S&P report said .
About 9,000 of the 10,650 excess deaths recorded during the 22-28 June heatwave were among those 65 and over, as rising heat exacerbated underlying conditions such as heart disease and dehydration.
“Beyond heat-related deaths, it’s also deteriorating health conditions and the resulting increase in treatment and hospitalisations that might weigh on re/insurers’ financials and, subsequently, increase premiums,” the report said.
A study in The Lancet Planetary Health recently found that people aged 60 and over face dangers from exposure to heat at much lower temperatures than previously thought. Older adults sweat less, their hearts work harder in the heat, and their blood vessels are less able to widen, limiting their capacity to stay cool.
In the UK alone, the four-day heatwave in May and eight-day heatwave in June together caused 2,877 excess deaths, compared with the 1,504 seen during the summer of 2025.

The ocean just broke a temperature record for what may be the first time in millennia.
Average daily global sea surface temperatures rose to nearly 70 degrees Fahrenheit last week, according to Monday data from the Copernicus Climate Change Service. 
“August 21st likely marked the warmest Sea Surface Temperatures have been for the entire Holocene period, and possibly even as far back as the last Interglacial 125,000 years ago,” University of Ottawa professor Ryan Katz-Rosene wrote in a post on X, reacting to the news.
That mark is up from the previous record of 69.2 degrees Fahrenheit set in 2024, which was the warmest year since record-keeping began in 1880.





The temperatures signal the impact of the coming super El Niño climate pattern, as well as warming from fossil fuel industry-driven climate change.

Copernicus noted that global ocean temperatures are typically the highest in March and April - not in August. 


That’s because that period follows the end of the warm summer season in the Southern Hemisphere.

More than 40 percent of the planet’s oceans are currently experiencing marine heat waves that threaten marine life and the global food supply, according to  data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Global sea surface temperatures reached unprecedented highs over the weekend and are expected to continue rising in the coming months, placing severe strain on life in the water and on land too, the European climate service Copernicus warned Monday.
Driven by a combination of human-induced climate change and a powerful El Nino phenomenon, sea temperatures touched 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) on Friday and Saturday. This slightly surpassed the previous daily average record recorded in March 2024, according to Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.
"This is yet another sign of our climate system under strain and the ocean under immense pressure," Burgess said.





Jane Lubchenco, an oceanographer and former chief of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, described the landmark warmth as "very troubling."
"An ocean this warm destabilizes weather patterns and threatens food security, economic prosperity and marine life," Lubchenco stated in an email, adding that "A warmer ocean is not our friend."

As oceans heat up, they lose oxygen and become increasingly acidic, threatening industries reliant on marine life, Burgess noted. The warming also disrupts atmospheric conditions and ocean currents, intensifying storms by increasing rainfall totals and storm surges.

Burgess explained that elevated marine temperatures worsen conditions on land during heatwaves. 
"When we have a warmer ocean such as we’ve had in Europe this summer, it amplifies the impact of heat waves because you don’t get the cooler nighttime temperatures with the sea breeze coming off the ocean when the ocean is very warm," she said.


Typically, global sea surface temperatures peak in March or April as the summer season in the Southern Hemisphere ends. However, the latest peak occurred in August. Burgess warned that temperatures will likely climb further until the current El Nino—a periodic warming of parts of the Pacific Ocean that impacts global climate patterns—reaches its height between November and January.



The active El Nino is already comparable in size to major past events and continues to intensify, with projections suggesting it could hit historic levels. While El Nino accounts for a significant portion of the current thermal spike, long-term warming driven by fossil fuel combustion has raised average water temperatures by 0.8 degrees Celsius (1.4 degrees Fahrenheit), Burgess added.

articles.title: Rail companies sued for £5m over oil spill caused by derailment
articles.raw_rss: More than 400,000 litres of fuel spilled in the area causing an "environmental disaster".
articles.raw_meta: More than 400,000 litres of fuel spilled in the area causing an "environmental disaster".
articles.jina_text:
Network Rail is suing two rail companies for more than £5m after a fuel spill caused by a train derailment threatened an "environmental disaster" at a designated site for protection.
The body filed a legal claim earlier this month against DB Cargo UK and Touax Rail over the derailment near Llangennech, Carmarthenshire, in August 2020.
The incident saw 10 wagons of the 25-wagon train derail, causing 446,000 litres of fuel to spill, and about 300 people had to leave the area due to the blaze.
In High Court documents, Network Rail claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" and is seeking damages for negligence.
No one was injured, but 116,000 litres of fuel ignited while 330,000 litres drained into surrounding wetlands, which form part of a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and a Special Area of Conservation.
The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) concluded in January 2022 that the derailment was caused by a set of wheels on one of the wagons locking, likely the result of a brake defect after "inadequate maintenance practices" were found in the investigation.
Network Rail, which owns, operates, maintains and develops Britain's railways, claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" by Touax. 




Image source, Adam Tilt
Image caption, 

It took firefighters nearly two days to put out the blaze




It is also seeking damages from DB Cargo UK, claiming that the latter "breached a contractual duty to ensure that reasonable care was taken" in maintaining the wagon.
Lawyers for the body said it expected to recover "more than £5m" with DB Cargo and Touax yet to file defences.
A hearing in the case is due to take place.
The locomotive was pulling the wagons from Milford Haven, Pembrokeshire, to Theale, near Reading, when the derailment occurred.
The line was closed for six months after the incident and did not fully reopen for almost a year, with 30,000 tonnes of fuel-soaked soil having to be excavated.




Image source, Getty Images
Image caption, 

The line closed for six months after the incident




Bill Kelly, the then-Network Rail Wales route director, said when the line fully reopened in March 2021 that work following the incident was "one of the biggest environmental recovery operations Network Rail has ever been involved with".
He added that the derailment could have caused a "total environmental disaster".
The RAIB said, in its 2022 report, that the train was travelling at about 38mph at the time of the derailment, and was carrying up to 75.5 tonnes of fuel.
The RAIB did not establish blame or liability for the incident, but made nine recommendations to avoid similar accidents.
Network Rail and DB Cargo declined to comment, while Touax has been approached for comment.

articles.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
articles.raw_rss: The record "is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress", according to Dr Samantha Burgess from the European Copernicus climate change service.
articles.raw_meta: The record "is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress", according to Dr Samantha Burgess from the European Copernicus climate change service.
articles.jina_text:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El Niño weather phenomenon.
The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.
That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.
Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.
"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.
"El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.


The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.














While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable. 
Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.
The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.
What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El Niño weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.
El Niño brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.
El Niño is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries.
This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further.
"The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El Niño is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton. 





"All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added. 


The waters far away from El Niño's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.
The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.
“This is unprecedented,” he added.
Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas.

Our climate is changing rapidly – and our politicians sound increasingly surreal

Zoe Williams






On a panel show last week, everyone in the audience wanted to talk about the climate emergency, but the lines rolled out by a Tory MP simply dissolved on contact with reality





As it is August, and everyone with stronger opinions is currently on holiday, last week I went on Any Questions?, the BBC Radio 4 panel show. I had prepared beforehand with a friend whose life’s work it is to make sure people don’t say anything stupid on the radio (or TV), and we’d talked about everything – the strait of Hormuz and energy prices; bus fare caps and the relative price of eggs; racism in the press and in public life; the AI bubble and the next financial crash; how many bathrooms Harry and Meghan currently have in the US, and whether a property even exists in the UK with that amount of toileting hardware.
Predictably, perhaps, the audience’s questions did not spread themselves neatly across the full suite of current affairs, though Harry and Meghan’s return did come up – it was more a matter of which question about the climate crisis best represented the fact that everyone wanted to talk about the climate crisis. The news had just dropped that El Niño would deliver us an unprecedentedly wet autumn, but that was unlikely to soothe the parched earth of the record-breakingly hot, dry summer. Crops are failing, the land is on fire and nobody has not noticed.



The question that best caught the mood was: “Have we left it too late to avert the crisis?” I said there was no such thing as too late, channelling the economist Ann Pettifor, one of the architects of the original Green New Deal, back in the 00s, when it looked as if some politicians, at least, were in the market for ideas. She argued that we had to proceed as though there was still hope, because the alternative – grim nihilism – was no basis for a cooperative, generative body politic, and however many degrees of warming we were facing, we’d need one of those. Isabel Hardman from the Spectator said that it was already too late for some things, and not for others. Things weren’t looking good for birch trees in the south and east of England, for instance. It was a sombre but not bitter point of difference.
Then the Conservative MP, Nigel Huddleston, came in. When detached from the phrase “net zero”, he seems like a reasonable, personable guy. But they’re not allowed to detach. Conservatives are tribally required to say that transforming to a carbon-neutral future is too expensive at this time. Hotter oceans exacerbate the sea level rise and extreme storms that threaten billions of people, as well as driving marine heatwaves that decimate sea life and undermine coastal livelihoods, scientists warned.

The northern hemisphere summer has already been hit by record-breaking heatwaves, drought and wildfires in Europe and North America, and intense rain and typhoons in Asia.


The ocean heat spike is being intensified by a fast developing El Niño event, which is set to be the hottest in at least a century. El Niño events are natural climate variations that raise global temperature and change weather patterns, with serious impacts around the world. The new El Niño has already delivered low monsoon rain in India, major wildfires in Indonesia and heightened fire concerns in Australia.
The new ocean heat record being set in August is especially remarkable as global sea temperatures are typically highest in March and April, after the austral summer. The southern hemisphere has significantly more ocean area than the northern.
“The record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Dr Samantha Burgess, at the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), which produced the new data. “El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming. The consequences are already visible: the number of marine heatwave days globally has more than tripled since the early 1990s.”
Warmer oceans contribute to sea level rise because of thermal expansion of the water, increasing flooding risks for coastal communities and low-lying island nations. Higher ocean temperatures also supercharge extreme weather events, because warmer seas transfer more energy and water vapour to the atmosphere, intensifying rainfall and storms.


Most of the planet-heating CO2 from fossil fuel burning and forest destruction is absorbed by the oceans. However, a hotter ocean is less efficient at absorbing CO2. This is potentially weakening one of the planet’s most important natural buffers against global heating, the scientists said.

This is not a natural calamity: it is being done to us knowingly

Tim Winton






Global heating is an outrage, not a tragedy. We deserve the facts about the climate crisis – I choose the Guardian because it’s one of the few places left to share them honestly 
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support 





Well, there’s no getting around it now. What many of us once feared has become a reality.
The dangerous conditions climate scientists long warned of have become our common, if deeply unwelcome, experience, and season by season, our acquaintance with disorder and extremities deepens. In both hemispheres, wildfires rage right into our cities and incinerate entire neighbourhoods. Marine heatwaves are bleaching corals and cooking seagrasses on a global scale. This northern summer has brought temperatures most Europeans associate with the Australian desert. Heat events in Europe have paralysed whole countries, destroyed infrastructure and killed citizens in their thousands.

Such is life at barely 1.5C of heating since pre-industrial times. We keep telling ourselves this is the new normal. But the awful truth is, we’re on track for nearly twice this. That’s tough to digest.
 
 
Climate campaign 2026: help the Guardian reach 30,000 acts of support 


In 2024, I published a novel, Juice, about a world that has lurched beyond even the horror zone of 3C of heating. Many readers told me the book was terrifying. Some felt it was prophetic. And while I appreciate having galvanised a few readers and helped them imagine the consequences of what’s still being done in our names, I hope to God they’re wrong about the book’s visionary aspect. Because the world of Juice is a nightmare. It’s what I fervently hope we will not pass on to our descendants.
My book was published into a strange cultural malaise from which we have not yet recovered. It feels like a debilitating communal illness whose symptoms include febrile delirium, visceral rage and a kind of nihilistic lassitude. But among the afflicted, you sense a terrible thirst and hear a babble of confusion, and also many plaintive cries of yearning. What sufferers thirst for is honest information. What they are addled by is the tide of bullshit that besets them. What they yearn for is solidarity and common purpose.

Can Burnham justify giving the go ahead to oil drilling? Yes, but these must be the conditions

Michael Jacobs






Carbon capture and storage could make the Rosebank site compatible with UK net zero commitments – if its owners are willing to pay the price





The British government must soon decide whether it should give consent to two oil and gasfields, Rosebank in the North Atlantic and Jackdaw in the North Sea. Amid both insecurity of energy supplies and deadly evidence of the climate crisis, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, is facing pressure from the oil and gas industry and unions on one side, and environmentalists on the other.
Labour’s manifesto commitment not to approve new drilling licences offers little help, because the fields already have licences, granted by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and 2023. But last year, Edinburgh’s court of session ruled that the environmental impact assessments on which this decision relied were unlawful. The Conservative government had, the court ruled, failed to include the emissions generated when the oil and gas from the fields is burned. The court allowed work to continue on the fields, but a new assessment had to be done and approval sought again.



The issue facing the new energy and climate secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is whether the additional information on the fields’ global emissions alters the grounds for consent.
Although invariably discussed together, the two fields are very different. Jackdaw is a small gasfield, with a production life of only 11 years. Its total carbon emissions will be only around 24m tonnes. Annually this would equate to around 0.8% of the UK’s total emissions. The gas would be piped into the UK, so would be consumed domestically. As this would probably displace dirtier liquified natural gas (LNG) imported from the US, it would make a small contribution to the UK’s energy security and emissions reduction.
By contrast, Rosebank is a large oilfield, with a 25-year life. During that time it would generate around 250m tonnes of carbon emissions. The oil would be sent to the Netherlands for refining, since the UK no longer has the appropriate capacity – and very little, if any, is likely to be used in the UK. So it would not contribute to our energy security.
There are good reasons, therefore, for the government to make different decisions on the two fields. Jackdaw can be justified (just) on energy security grounds. How does El Niño affect our weather? | Decomplicated


El Nino describes the warming of sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean, occurring every few years.
The phenomenon disrupts weather patterns globally, while the last El Nino intensified global heat and led to severe droughts, flooding, marine heatwaves and coral bleaching.
US meteorologists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration declared the start of an El Nino event in June, predicting it could last until spring 2027. 
Forecasts have suggested that this El Nino will end up being the strongest on record, while experts have said 2027 could be the hottest year on record as a result of the unprecedented event. 
Dr Nick Dunstone, Met Office science fellow, said: “During large El Nino events significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere, leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Nino.”

According to DESNZ's own analysis, each direct position in the industry sustains an additional 4.4 jobs throughout the wider supply chain across the country.

articles.jina_text:
Sewage has been dumped hundreds of times at bathing sites this summer, making much of Britain’s waters potentially unsafe to swim in during one of the hottest, driest summers on record. 
Since the start of the official bathing season on 15 May, the charity Surfers Against Sewage has recorded 764 sewage alerts at 244 bathing spots in England and Wales. 
This means 43 per cent of the 573 bathing spots in England and Wales have had sewage warnings so far this year. The bathing season ends on 30 September this year.

 
Sewage alerts are triggered when real-time water company data shows a firm is dumping sewage or when Environment Agency modelling triggers a warning of pollution, typically after heavy rainfall. 
Spittal Beach in Northumberland had the highest number of alerts, with 11 warnings in total, followed by Sandy Gap Beach and Biggar Bank Beach on Cumbria’s Walney Island, both of which triggered 10 alerts since May. 
Many of the worst-performing bathing spots are in the north-west, where there has been more rain. 

 
  
A number of sites along the south coast have also seen over six alerts triggered, despite the minimal amount of rain there since June.



 
‘Public health crisis’ 
Water companies are allowed to discharge sewage during periods of extreme rainfall to prevent their pipe networks from becoming overwhelmed and sewage backing up into people’s homes. 
However, they also regularly dump sewage during dry weather or following minimal rainfall. Sewage was discharged in the Cornish town of Fowey this weekend despite the area experiencing only light rain showers. South West Water said the discharges were due to “pumps not keeping up” with tidal water entering the sewer. 
It’s not clear from Surfers Against Sewage’s data which of these alerts followed periods of heavy rainfall. All regions of England have experienced some heavy rainfall this summer, particularly in early June. However, much of the south and east of the country experienced virtually no rainfall in July and early August. 
Kirsty Davies, community water quality manager at Surfers Against Sewage, said it was “shocking” that over 700 sewage alerts had been triggered in the space of a few months. 
She said the ongoing sewage pollution has led to issues including “families getting sick after a day at the beach, swimming events cancelled, holidaymakers suffering infections from dirty water”. 
Gastroenteritis is typically one of the most common illnesses experienced by people swimming in polluted water. It can be caused when people swallow water contaminated with bacteria such as E.coli. Other issues include skin, eye and throat infections. 
“This is a public health crisis caused by water company mismanagement and greed, and the Government is cowering away from any responsibility to protect public health,” Davies said.

articles.jina_text:
Air conditioning units hang on the facade of a residential building in Seville, southern Spain. Photograph: Cristina Quicler/AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Air conditioning units hang on the facade of a residential building in Seville, southern Spain. Photograph: Cristina Quicler/AFP/Getty Images


Air conditioning push favoured over emissions cuts in six European nations, survey finds


Poll also finds sizeable majorities who believe it should be easier to install air con in homes




Given the choice, more people across six major European nations including the UK favour encouraging the adoption of air conditioning over keeping carbon emissions down, a survey has found.
After four extreme heatwaves that have caused thousands of excess deaths across the continent, the survey showed between 30% and 52% of people in six countries had feared for their household’s health in temperatures close to or above 40C (104F).

Large numbers of people, ranging from 27% in Spain to 41% in France and 53% in Germany, said they felt they could not keep their homes cool enough, and many wanted governments to explore a variety of ways to help make them more comfortable.

The YouGov polling, carried out in mid-July in France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Spain and in early August in the UK, found that between 61% and 73% of respondents favoured air conditioning being installed as standard in all new homes.


A further 65% to 75% backed making it easier for people to install air conditioning without needing permission from local councils or landlords, and between 52% and 66% said they would support government subsidies for homeowners to have it installed.
In every country except Italy, significantly more people – between 41% and 48% – said allowing and encouraging more air conditioning to reduce harms from heatwaves should be prioritised over lowering CO2 emissions, with 20% to 33% believing the reverse.
In all countries, more people thought more air conditioning would have a very or fairly large impact on reducing harms from heatwaves (29% to 61%) than that it would have a very or fairly large impact on their country’s climate figures (19% to 40%).
Air conditioning is much less common in Europe than in the US, where 93% of people have a central or portable system. The poll put take-up at 63% in Italy and 58% in Spain, but only 30% in France, 23% in Poland, 16% in Germany and 11% in the UK.
Those figures do not reflect broad opposition to air conditioning, however, with attitudes mainly positive (46% to 60%) or neutral (31% to 39%). France was an outlier, with 20% hostile, and left-leaning voters notably more negative than elsewhere.



Air conditioning has become a new front in Europe’s culture wars, with mainstream parties accused of blocking its large-scale use on “ideological” green grounds, and far-right parties, which are broadly opposed to combating the climate crisis, pushing it as vital.

Stores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaning

Dave Schilling






Capitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spice





Happy spooky season, everyone! Get those jack-o’-lanterns out, because Halloween is just around the corner!
Just kidding, no, it’s not.

It’s August, for God’s sake. Every day, I wake up to 90F weather – my skin moist with sweat and my eyelids stuck together. I can’t drink coffee on my porch without being consumed by an army of voracious mosquitoes that seem to find my blood to be the most delicious of all.
And it’s not just Los Angeles that’s withering under a summer of discontent. The east coast heatwaves are piling up, sending millions of young people to the absolute last place they want to be: an air-conditioned movie theater. But you want to tell me it’s fine to be putting out Halloween decorations? If I don’t store my giant bag of fun-size Twix in a standup freezer, the whole damn thing will melt into chocolate soup. (Don’t even get me started on recent claims you should eat soup when it’s hot outside. It’d rather slurp up my own sweat from a bowl.)






Halloween is no ungodly American import – just ask the medieval monks and nuns who marketed it
Michael Carter


Read more
Why am I fuming about this? Even though I love Halloween, I’m mad because our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun. In August. I find all of that unacceptable. It feels like a violation of the natural order, a realignment of one of the few glorious constants left in the world. I yearn to go back to the tidy order of holidays, where no two ever cross paths. At most, Halloween celebrations should start in late September. Not a month after Independence Day. I fear those days are done, that our world has irrevocably changed and I need to start getting ready to give in to the new normal.
I first became aware of Halloween’s creep into the summer during a recent sundries run at Target. There are costumes, life-size skeletons, treats and various decorations on offer in-store. I’ve seen massive candy bags positioned to move at CVS. There’s even a smattering of greeting cards, which I find doubly frustrating, as I’ve never in my life considered buying someone a card for Halloween, a holiday that most adults spend binge drinking or squeezing into provocative outfits. What does a Halloween greeting card even say? “I Boo-lieve You Should Get an Uber Home”? “Have a Spooktacular One-Night Stand With Your Marginally Attractive Co-Worker”?

London’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air?


Similar initiatives have been launched from Barcelona to Bogotá, but they have misinformation, political pressure and vested interests stacked against them




Ten years ago, Alastair Harper was an advocate for young people’s health sitting in a stuffy meeting room in London planning an air pollution campaign. “My phone started buzzing,” he said. “I took the call, and then told the room I needed to leave immediately.
“I had to get to UCLH [one of London’s major hospitals]. My own child was headed there in a blue-lit ambulance because she was struggling to breathe London’s toxic air.”

Hundreds of thousands of parents across the UK capital had similar experiences in those years. Between about 6,000 and 8,000 people were dying prematurely each year in London in the late 2010s. In 2020, an inquest found that the death of Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah in 2013 had been a direct result of air pollution, the first time it had been listed as a cause of death in the UK.


View image in fullscreen
Commuters cross London Bridge on a smoggy morning in 2012.  Photograph: Barry Lewis/Corbis/Getty Images
This week, a study from Queen Mary University London (QMUL) showed a significant reversal. Children’s lungs had grown bigger and stronger since the most polluting vehicles have been restricted on the capital’s roads, scientists found. The ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) – introduced by London’s mayor Sadiq Khan in 2019 and expanded in 2021 and 2023 – charges £12.50 a day for more polluting vehicles that do not meet stringent standards. It has drastically cut levels of nitrogen dioxide, a harmful pollutant.


To Harper, who later worked for Khan as an environmental adviser, and now works independently, relief at his own child’s recovery has been supplemented by the satisfaction of knowing that far fewer parents will experience such dread. “To know now that same air is so much safer for the kids that breathe it because of the political choice of one man makes me feel proud of this city,” he said.
Nick Hopkinson, a professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London, said the QMUL study was not a surprise. “There is an absolute wealth of evidence that air pollution is a major cause of ill health and premature death across the planet,” he said. Air pollution kills 7 million people a year globally, according to the World Health Organization.

articles.jina_text:
Plans for new onshore windfarms in England have reached their highest annual level in a decade, after the government overturned the Conservatives’ de facto ban in 2015.
About 45 applications for new onshore windfarms were submitted in the year to March,according to a Guardian analysis of government data.

Onshore wind power capacity entering the planning system has more than tripled since Labour dropped the blocks on onshore developments within days of coming to power just over two years ago, the analysis revealed.
Before the party’s election victory, applications for about 9 megawatts of onshore wind were submitted in England each month on a 12-month rolling average basis. But by the beginning of this year that rate reached about 36MW a month, according to the data, as renewable energy developers began to return to England.
The onshore wind resurgence is even greater when compared with the nadir of onshore wind in England in the months before September 2023, when Conservative ministers first began to loosen the regulatory red tape on onshore wind developments.

Then, onshore wind applications averaged about 1MW a month. At the time, the Guardian revealed that Ukraine was completing more onshore windfarms than England, even as it was occupied by Russian soldiers.


A government spokesperson said: “For too long, a de facto ban held back onshore wind in England, despite its potential to strengthen our energy security, grow the economy and get bills down for good.
“That is why we lifted the ban, backed the largest onshore windfarm in England in a decade through our flagship renewables auction, and made it easier for farms and factories to install a single small turbine – no bigger than an oak tree – without needing planning permission.”







UK backs biggest English onshore windfarm in a decade among 190 green energy projects

Read more
The Imerys project, near St Austell, Cornwall, became the largest onshore windfarm in England to secure a government subsidy since the ban was lifted earlier this year. The 20MW project is dwarfed by many Scottish onshore windfarms, and underlines the trend for smaller windfarms in England since the ban was lifted.
The Guardian’s analysis shows that since the onshore ban was lifted, the average onshore windfarm proposed in England had just two turbines, delivering 8MW of renewable power capacity. In Scotland, the average onshore windfarm proposed over the same period had nine turbines, with 59MW of capacity.
Only one windfarm with a capacity above 100MW has been proposed in England since the onshore ban was lifted. Meanwhile, there have been 18 onshore windfarms with a capacity greater than 100MW proposed in Scotland over the same period.


In total, England’s onshore wind proposals since the ban was lifted have climbed to 438MW, compared with applications totalling 490MW in Wales and 5,280MW in Scotland over the same period.

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the Government needs to “do more to improve and modernise buildings”, including a “focus on ventilation, solar panels, improved insulation, measures to ensure buildings are watertight and potentially air conditioning too”. 
The Government set out updated standards for new and refurbished school buildings in England in February, but they do not include mandatory air conditioning. 
Instead, they emphasise overheating risk assessments and require ground-source heat pumps to be installed to deliver cooling.  
More than a third of schools in England do not have air conditioning, according to Department for Education (DfE) data obtained by Tes. 
Cuts to building maintenance funding 
The Climate Change Committee said using heat pumps to provide “active cooling” would be acceptable in lieu of air conditioning, but education leaders warned that more funding was needed to roll out the measures. 
The DfE said it is equipping schools to deal with heatwaves via its £710m renewal and retrofit programme through to 2029-30 and almost £20bn through 2034-35 to rebuild over 750 schools.



 
Whiteman said additional funding was needed to ensure schools are “future-proofed against the risks of climate change”.

articles.title: Welsh county becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
articles.raw_rss: The smell of burning from the Blaenavon wildfire was reported 30 miles away in Cardiff.
articles.raw_meta: The smell of burning from the Blaenavon wildfire was reported 30 miles away in Cardiff.
articles.jina_text:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.
The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.
Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data, external published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ávila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July. 
Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".
A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.
Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared, which eventually required assistance from the military.
Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.
"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."
Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

"These conditions are not only frightening - they carry serious health consequences for children whose bodies and lungs are still developing."
Torfaen council said it was not aware of the research and "it is not clear what data or evidence was used in the assessment to arrive at the reported conclusion".
It said it "recognises that prolonged wildfire incidents have the potential to adversely affect local air quality, particularly through increased levels of smoke and particulate matter".
It added it "continuously monitors" air quality through a monitoring station in Croesyceiliog Cwmbran.

articles.title: Council set to axe climate emergency declaration
articles.raw_rss: Barnsley Council says a review is under way to asses climate and net zero-related activity.
articles.raw_meta: Barnsley Council says a review is under way to asses climate and net zero-related activity.
articles.jina_text:
The party said a review of all climate and net-zero activity was under way, saying programmes that lacked a clear resident benefit, financial saving or statutory requirement should change or stop.
The council's intention is to withdraw the Climate Emergency declaration from 2019, Zero40, Zero45 and similar net-zero targets, and to direct resources to frontline services.
Council leader William Brown said: "Our focus is on practical priorities that matter to residents, rather than ideological targets and costly political posturing."
Through the Climate Change Act, the UK is obliged by law to reach net zero, nationally, by 2050.
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, according to the United Nations' climate body.
'War on woke'
Zero40 is Barnsley Council's environmental strategy aiming for the authority's operations and carbon emissions to reach net zero by 2040, while Zero45 is its strategy to make the entire borough net zero by 2045, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.














A report from 2024 stated the council was not "on track" to reduce its carbon emissions.
Brown said the council would continue to back practical work that delivered clear benefits for residents and businesses.
This includes activity that helps households cut energy bills, improves the energy efficiency of homes and council buildings, reduces long-term running costs, supports local businesses, secures external funding for the borough or is needed to meet statutory duties.
"The war on woke is only just beginning. We have taken the first steps, but there is much more to do," he said.
"We have stood up for our countryside, got the bins back on track and we are standing firm on our intention to withdraw the climate emergency declaration."
An initial report will be completed by the end of September.
Earlier this year, Reform-led Wakefield Council voted to rescind its climate and biodiversity emergency declaration from May 2019.
Other Reform-led councils such as Newcastle-under-Lyme Borough Council, Sunderland Council, South Tyneside Council and Walsall Council also backed a motion to rescind the pledges.

An unusually high number of jellyfish are crowding Delaware’s beaches this summer amid climate change and other environmental factors – keeping some beachgoers out of the ocean and stinging lifeguards as well as bathers.
Beach safety patrols in the state have reported hundreds of daily stings as the jellyfish have increased with intensifying environmental factors, including warmer waters, hot and dry conditions, and water circulation favorable to the invertebrates.

Jellyfish have been spotted in the water and washed ashore across popular beach destinations, including South Bethany Beach, Rehoboth Beach, Dewey Beach and Lewes Beach, and the frequency of stings has alarmed beachlovers.
Nico Caceres, the Rehoboth Beach patrol captain said in an interview: “The jellyfish for the past couple weeks have been very plentiful … The type of stings we’re seeing this summer, we haven’t really seen in past summers.”
Caceres, who has been stung “plenty of times” himself, explained that the effect of stings he has typically seen in past seasons last between 30 and 45 minutes, but that this summer’s stings have caused pain and other symptoms lasting an entire day.
“We have been seeing a lot of smaller children who actually end up vomiting a lot,” Caceres said. Along with many beachgoers, the lifeguards on his team who have also been stung have been avoiding going into the water out of concern about being stung again.
“People think we close the water because no one’s going in, but it’s just because people don’t want to get stung. It’s pretty much a guarantee you’ll get stung if you go,” he said, adding that since the end of July, his team has recorded between 150 and 200 stings a day.
Braden Jones, a lifeguard at Lewes Beach, also noted plenty of stings, averaging about 100 a day.


View image in fullscreen
Lewes Beach lifeguard Braden Jones Photograph: Maya Yang/The Guardian
“It gets to the highest around the afternoon,” Jones told the Guardian from his lifeguard chair, adding that he has been seeing beachgoers go in the water less this summer and “staying away from the jellyfish”.
Jones, who himself has gotten stung before, described the sensation as a “stinging pain” that then gets itchy.

The term “El Nino” has dominated headlines in recent weeks as much of the world struggles to cope with extreme weather.
US meteorologists announced the return of the phenomenon earlier this summer, warning it could contribute to record global temperatures and the hottest year ever recorded in 2027.
Here the Independent examines what El Nino is, how it interacts with human-driven climate change, and how it is currently affecting weather conditions across the UK.

What is El Nino?
El Nino – which means “little boy” in Spanish – is widely used to describe the warming of sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean that occurs every few years.





The phenomenon typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts several months.
